subtopic_detail: Food bolus impaction in a young atopic adult with rings and furrows at endoscopy
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar who has just endoscopically relieved a food bolus impaction in a 26 year old man who could not swallow his own saliva after eating steak. The bolus was pushed through without complication.

He tells you that solid food has caught in his chest intermittently for two years, that he always sits at the end of the table so he can drink water with every mouthful, and that he cuts meat very small. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid and seasonal hay fever. Liquids have never been a problem.

data_table.Endoscopic findings: Concentric rings throughout the oesophageal body with linear longitudinal furrows and scattered white exudate, no stricture and no mass, normal stomach and duodenum
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), other indices within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform balloon dilatation of the oesophagus at the same procedure
options.rationale: Dilatation relieves dysphagia from fibrostenotic disease and is used later in management, but performing it immediately after a traumatic bolus removal increases the risk of mucosal tear and perforation. It also treats the calibre without establishing the inflammatory diagnosis that determines ongoing therapy. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor and arrange review in 8 weeks
options.rationale: High dose acid suppression is a legitimate first line treatment and induces remission in a proportion of patients, but treating before biopsies are taken removes the histological baseline against which response is judged. Since the diagnosis requires 15 or more eosinophils per high power field, starting treatment first can obscure it entirely. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow to define the length of the narrowing
options.rationale: Contrast studies can show a small calibre oesophagus or a subtle stricture, which is useful when planning dilatation, but they cannot demonstrate mucosal eosinophilia. The endoscopic appearance has already characterised the oesophagus better than barium would. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Refer for skin prick allergy testing to guide an elimination diet
options.rationale: Skin prick and specific IgE testing correlate poorly with the foods that actually drive this disease, so allergy directed elimination performs worse than empirical elimination of common trigger groups. Dietary therapy is also a treatment decision that follows the diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Take multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal sites
options.rationale: Eosinophilic infiltration is patchy, so at least six biopsies are taken from both the proximal and distal oesophagus to reach adequate sensitivity, and the diagnosis rests on 15 or more eosinophils per high power field. Biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal, because up to a fifth of affected patients have no endoscopic abnormality at all. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is the commonest cause of food bolus impaction in young adults and typically presents with years of solid food dysphagia and adaptive eating behaviours that patients do not report unless asked, such as cutting food very small, chewing excessively, drinking with every mouthful and avoiding meat and bread. It is strongly associated with atopy, and the endoscopic signature is concentric rings, linear furrows, white exudates and a small calibre oesophagus, although the mucosa is normal in a significant minority. Diagnosis is histological and requires multiple biopsies from two levels because the infiltrate is patchy. Treatment rests on three pillars, namely proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids and dietary elimination, with dilatation reserved for fibrostenotic disease, and untreated inflammation progresses to fibrosis and stricture over years.
key_points: Commonest cause of food bolus impaction in young adults
At least six biopsies from proximal and distal oesophagus, even if the mucosa looks normal
Diagnosis requires 15 or more eosinophils per high power field
Allergy testing correlates poorly with the responsible foods
Untreated inflammation progresses to fibrostenotic disease over years
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about eating behaviours rather than about dysphagia: a young adult who drinks water with every mouthful, avoids bread and steak, or is always last to finish a meal has been adapting to a narrowed oesophagus for years.

subtopic_detail: Abrupt creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor in a man with widespread atherosclerosis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 72 year old man two weeks after starting perindopril 5 mg daily for blood pressure that had remained high on amlodipine. He feels well and has taken every dose.

He smoked 40 pack years, has calf claudication at 200 metres and had a coronary stent 3 years ago. He has twice been admitted overnight with sudden breathlessness that settled quickly with diuretic. He takes no anti-inflammatory medicines and has not been vomiting or had diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, mucous membranes moist, audible bruit in the left upper abdomen, absent posterior tibial pulses bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L, up from 98 micromol/L six weeks ago (60 to 110), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22 to 32), urine dipstick trace protein and no blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue perindopril and add frusemide 40 mg daily for the oedema
options.rationale: He is euvolaemic with a normal jugular venous pressure, a clear chest and no peripheral oedema, so there is no oedema to treat. Adding a diuretic to a patient with a rapidly rising creatinine reduces renal perfusion further and worsens the injury. (Source: KHA-CARI: Chronic kidney disease management)

options.text: Cease perindopril and recheck creatinine and potassium in one week
options.rationale: A creatinine rise of more than about 30 per cent within weeks of starting a renin angiotensin system blocker indicates that glomerular filtration in that patient depends on angiotensin mediated efferent arteriolar tone, which is the hallmark of critical bilateral renal artery stenosis in a man with this vascular history. Withdrawal usually reverses the injury within days, and the biochemistry is repeated to confirm recovery before any further investigation. (Source: KHA-CARI: Chronic kidney disease management)

options.text: Refer for renal artery angioplasty and stenting within two weeks
options.rationale: Randomised trials have shown that revascularisation of atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis does not improve renal function, blood pressure control or mortality compared with medical therapy, and it carries risks of dissection and atheroembolism. It is reserved for refractory hypertension, rapidly deteriorating function despite medical treatment or recurrent flash pulmonary oedema. (Source: KHA-CARI: Chronic kidney disease management)

options.text: Continue perindopril and arrange a renal tract ultrasound this week
options.rationale: Imaging to look for asymmetrical kidney size and to assess the renal arteries is a reasonable subsequent step, but continuing the drug while waiting allows the injury to progress over days. The offending agent is withdrawn first and investigation follows. (Source: KHA-CARI: Chronic kidney disease management)

options.text: Halve the perindopril dose and repeat the blood tests in one month
options.rationale: Dose reduction may partially relieve the haemodynamic effect but leaves an already hyperkalaemic patient with a near doubled creatinine on the responsible drug. A month is far too long an interval when potassium is 5.4 mmol/L and rising. (Source: KHA-CARI: Chronic kidney disease management)

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers dilate the efferent arteriole, which lowers intraglomerular pressure and is the mechanism behind their long term renoprotective effect. A small creatinine rise of up to about 30 per cent after starting one is expected, is haemodynamic rather than structural, and is not a reason to stop. A larger or progressive rise signals that filtration was dependent on efferent tone, which occurs in critical bilateral renal artery stenosis, stenosis in a single functioning kidney, volume depletion, concurrent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use and severe heart failure. Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema in a hypertensive patient with widespread atherosclerosis is a classic clue to bilateral disease. Revascularisation has repeatedly failed to outperform medical therapy in randomised trials, so management centres on withdrawal of the precipitant, cardiovascular risk reduction and blood pressure control with agents that do not depend on the renin angiotensin axis.
key_points: A creatinine rise up to 30 per cent after starting these agents is expected and not a reason to stop
A larger rise suggests filtration dependent on efferent arteriolar tone
Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with widespread atherosclerosis suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis
Revascularisation has not improved outcomes over medical therapy in randomised trials
Withdraw the precipitant first, then investigate
explanation.pearls: Check creatinine and potassium 1 to 2 weeks after starting or uptitrating any renin angiotensin system blocker, and treat a rise beyond 30 per cent or a potassium above 5.5 mmol/L as a signal to stop and reassess rather than to persist and monitor.

subtopic_detail: Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation with localised bone pain and cortical thickening
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 68 year old man with 6 months of deep aching in his right shin that is worse at night and not related to activity. He has also noticed his hats feel tighter and his hearing has declined on the right.

He takes no regular medications and has had no fractures, no weight loss and no fevers. He worked as a plumber and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Anterolateral bowing of the right tibia with skin warmth over the shin, no joint effusion, no localised tenderness suggesting fracture, Weber test lateralises to the left
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 640 units/L (30 to 110), gamma glutamyl transferase 28 units/L (less than 50), ALT 22 units/L (less than 40), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (more than 50), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60 to 110)
data_table.Imaging: Tibial radiograph shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae and bowing, nuclear bone scan shows intense uptake in the right tibia and right hemipelvis only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence regular paracetamol and review the pain in three months
options.rationale: Analgesia alone controls symptoms without suppressing the accelerated bone turnover that produces bowing, deafness, secondary osteoarthritis and, rarely, high output cardiac failure. It is appropriate only for the patient who cannot receive bone specific therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months
options.rationale: Denosumab is an effective antiresorptive for osteoporosis but is not the established treatment for this disorder, where intravenous bisphosphonate produces prolonged biochemical remission after a single dose. Denosumab also requires uninterrupted six monthly dosing, since cessation causes rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a single intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg
options.rationale: A raised alkaline phosphatase with normal liver enzymes, localised bone pain and radiographic cortical thickening with coarse trabeculae indicates accelerated disordered bone remodelling, and a single zoledronic acid infusion normalises turnover in the great majority with remission lasting years. His vitamin D is replete and his renal function normal, which are the two checks required before infusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for bone biopsy of the tibial lesion before any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated when the radiographic appearance is atypical or when sarcomatous change is suspected, signalled by rapidly increasing pain, a soft tissue mass or cortical destruction. The imaging here is characteristic and biopsy would add procedural risk without changing management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start calcium and colecalciferol supplements and repeat the ALP
options.rationale: Vitamin D repletion and adequate calcium intake are required before bisphosphonate treatment to prevent hypocalcaemia, and both are already satisfactory here. Offered as the treatment they address osteomalacia, which is the near pair to separate: osteomalacia also raises alkaline phosphatase but does so with low vitamin D, low or low normal calcium and low phosphate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of accelerated, disorganised bone remodelling that most often affects the pelvis, femur, tibia, spine and skull, and it is frequently found incidentally through an isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation. When symptomatic it causes deep bone pain, bowing deformity, secondary osteoarthritis in adjacent joints, and skull involvement producing increasing hat size and hearing loss through cochlear and eighth nerve involvement. The first diagnostic step is to confirm the alkaline phosphatase is of bone origin by checking gamma glutamyl transferase, which is normal in bone disease and raised in cholestatic liver disease. Nuclear bone scanning defines the extent of skeletal involvement, while plain radiographs of affected sites confirm the characteristic appearance and exclude other lesions. Treatment indications are symptomatic disease, involvement of sites at risk of complications such as skull or weight bearing long bones, and planned surgery at an affected site, and a single zoledronic acid infusion is the standard approach.
key_points: A normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase is of bone origin
Skull involvement causes increasing hat size and sensorineural hearing loss
Nuclear bone scan maps the extent of disease, plain films confirm the appearance
A single zoledronic acid infusion gives prolonged biochemical remission
Check vitamin D and renal function before any intravenous bisphosphonate
explanation.pearls: New, rapidly worsening pain at a previously stable Paget site, especially with a soft tissue mass, suggests osteosarcoma, which develops in under 1 per cent but carries a very poor prognosis and needs urgent imaging rather than escalation of analgesia.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

subtopic_detail: Second recurrence of toxigenic Clostridioides difficile colitis after vancomycin treatment
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74 year old woman with a third episode of watery diarrhoea, now eight times a day with lower abdominal cramping. The first episode followed ceftriaxone for pneumonia four months ago and was treated with oral metronidazole; the second, six weeks ago, settled on a ten day course of oral vancomycin.

Each time her symptoms returned within two weeks of finishing treatment. She has taken no antibiotics since and lives independently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness, no guarding or rigidity, bowel sounds present, no abdominal distension
data_table.Investigations: Stool toxin gene detected by nucleic acid amplification with toxin detected on enzyme immunoassay, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45 to 90), albumin 34 g/L (35 to 50), lactate 1.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin 1 g twice daily for ten days
options.rationale: Vancomycin given intravenously is not excreted into the bowel lumen in therapeutic concentrations, so it has no activity against colonic infection. The route is the entire point: oral vancomycin works because it is not absorbed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat the ten day course of oral metronidazole 400 mg 8 hourly
options.rationale: Metronidazole has lower cure rates than vancomycin and fidaxomicin and is no longer recommended for recurrent disease, being reserved for mild first episodes where the other agents are unavailable. Repeating an agent that already failed at the first episode predicts a further recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe loperamide to control the stool frequency and review
options.rationale: Antimotility agents impair clearance of toxin from the colon and have been associated with progression to toxic megacolon in this infection. Symptom control without antimicrobial treatment leaves the organism and its toxin in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for ten days
options.rationale: Fidaxomicin has a narrow spectrum that preserves the protective anaerobic gut flora, and it produces substantially fewer recurrences than vancomycin, which is why it is preferred for a first or subsequent recurrence. A tapered and pulsed oral vancomycin regimen is the alternative when fidaxomicin is unavailable, and faecal microbiota transplantation is considered after multiple recurrences. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat stool toxin testing at the end of treatment to confirm cure
options.rationale: Test of cure is explicitly not recommended because the toxin gene and even toxin remain detectable for weeks in patients who have responded clinically, generating unnecessary re-treatment. Response is judged by resolution of diarrhoea. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Clostridioides difficile infection follows disruption of the colonic microbiota, most often by antibiotics, and recurrence affects roughly a quarter of patients after a first episode, with the risk rising sharply after each subsequent one. Recurrence usually represents persistence of spores rather than treatment failure of the vegetative organism, which is why the therapeutic strategy shifts from simply killing the organism towards preserving and restoring the microbiota. Fidaxomicin achieves this with its narrow spectrum and is the preferred agent for recurrence in Australian guidance, with tapered and pulsed vancomycin as an alternative and faecal microbiota transplantation for multiple recurrences. Severity assessment runs in parallel and looks for hypotension, ileus, megacolon, a white cell count above 15 x10^9/L, a rising creatinine and a lactate above 2.2 mmol/L, since fulminant disease needs surgical involvement. Proton pump inhibitors and unnecessary antibiotics should be stopped where possible because both increase recurrence risk.
key_points: Fidaxomicin is preferred for recurrence because it spares protective gut flora
Intravenous vancomycin has no activity in the colonic lumen
Antimotility agents risk toxic megacolon and are avoided
Test of cure is not performed, since toxin remains detectable after clinical recovery
Faecal microbiota transplantation is considered after multiple recurrences
explanation.pearls: Review and stop the proton pump inhibitor in anyone with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection where there is no clear ongoing indication, as acid suppression is one of the few modifiable risk factors for further recurrence.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Antimicrobial stewardship

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis emerging on long term amiodarone with absent vascularity on colour flow Doppler
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66 year old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for 3 years to maintain sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation ablation. Over the past 3 months he has lost 7 kg without trying, feels his heart racing, and his atrial fibrillation has returned.

He has never had thyroid disease and no one in his family has. He has not travelled and has not taken any iodine containing supplement or had contrast imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 138/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No palpable goitre and no thyroid bruit, no proptosis, lid retraction or ophthalmoplegia, no pretibial changes, fine tremor present
data_table.Investigations: TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 42 pmol/L (9 to 25), free T3 9.8 pmol/L (3.0 to 5.5), TSH receptor antibody negative, C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Thyroid ultrasound: Normal gland volume with no nodule, colour flow Doppler shows absent intrathyroidal vascularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and monitor thyroid function
options.rationale: Absent vascularity on colour flow Doppler, a normal non-nodular gland and negative receptor antibodies indicate a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone rather than increased synthesis, and corticosteroid is the effective treatment for that mechanism. Response is typically apparent within one to two weeks, which also serves to confirm the mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence carbimazole 40 mg daily and monitor thyroid function
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are the treatment for the iodine induced hypersynthetic form, which occurs in a gland with underlying nodularity or autonomy and shows increased vascularity on Doppler. In a destructive thyroiditis there is no ongoing synthesis to block, since the hormone has already been made and is leaking from damaged follicles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland now
options.rationale: Radioiodine requires the gland to take up iodine, and the massive iodine load from amiodarone suppresses uptake for many months, so the treatment simply fails. Radioiodine uptake is characteristically very low in both forms of amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease amiodarone alone and recheck thyroid function in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Whether to stop amiodarone is a separate cardiological decision, and stopping it does not resolve the thyrotoxicosis quickly because the drug has a half life measured in months and is stored in adipose tissue. Waiting 6 weeks leaves an older man in thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation without treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for urgent total thyroidectomy under cardiac anaesthesia
options.rationale: Thyroidectomy is definitive and is used when medical treatment fails, when the type cannot be determined and mixed treatment is ineffective, or when cardiac decompensation demands immediate resolution. It is not the first line approach when a clearly identified destructive process is likely to respond to corticosteroid within weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains roughly 37 per cent iodine by weight and one 200 mg tablet delivers many times the recommended daily iodine intake, which is why it disturbs thyroid function in a substantial minority of users. Thyrotoxicosis on amiodarone comes in two forms that require opposite treatments. Type 1 is iodine induced excess synthesis in a gland with pre-existing nodularity or latent Graves disease, shows increased vascularity on colour flow Doppler and responds to thionamides. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis in a previously normal gland, shows absent or reduced vascularity with a modestly raised C reactive protein, responds to corticosteroid, and occurs in mixed forms that require both treatments. Radioiodine uptake is low in both because of the iodine load, so it has no role, and because amiodarone has a half life of months the thyrotoxicosis persists long after the drug is stopped, with beta blockade used for symptom control throughout.
key_points: Type 1 is excess synthesis in an abnormal gland with increased Doppler vascularity, treated with thionamides
Type 2 is destructive thyroiditis in a normal gland with absent vascularity, treated with corticosteroid
Radioiodine fails in both because the iodine load suppresses uptake
Amiodarone's half life of months means stopping it does not resolve the problem quickly
Thyroidectomy is reserved for failure of medical therapy or cardiac decompensation
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function before starting amiodarone and every 6 months thereafter, and continue checking for up to 12 months after it is stopped, because the drug and its iodine load persist in adipose tissue long after the last dose.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Amiodarone induced thyroid dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Acute flaccid paralysis with profound hypokalaemia after a carbohydrate load in an untreated thyrotoxic man
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 28 year old man who woke at 5 am unable to lift his legs off the bed and only just able to raise his arms. Power has been returning slowly over the past hour.

Last night he trained heavily at the gym and then ate a large rice and noodle meal. He had a milder episode three months ago that resolved by itself before he reached a doctor. He takes no medications, no supplements and no diuretics, and has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. He has lost 5 kg over 6 months and feels hot at night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness, power 2 out of 5 in the legs and 4 out of 5 in the arms, reflexes depressed, sensation intact throughout, no goitre palpable, no eye signs, fine tremor present
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium 0.85 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 to 32), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 38 pmol/L (9 to 25)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with prominent U waves and a prolonged QU interval, no arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 60 mmol of oral potassium chloride immediately and repeat
options.rationale: Large potassium loads are the specific hazard in this syndrome, because total body potassium is normal and the deficit is a shift into cells that reverses spontaneously as the episode resolves. Aggressive replacement is followed by rebound hyperkalaemia in a substantial proportion of patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes
options.rationale: Magnesium replacement is essential when hypokalaemia is refractory because of concurrent magnesium depletion, and his magnesium is normal at 0.85 mmol/L. Correcting a normal value does nothing for an intracellular shift. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence carbimazole alone and await the potassium to correct
options.rationale: Treating the underlying thyrotoxicosis is essential and prevents further attacks, but thionamides take weeks to render a patient euthyroid and do nothing for a potassium of 2.1 mmol/L with U waves today. It is the right long term answer to the wrong immediate question. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give cautious potassium replacement with propranolol and monitor
options.rationale: The paralysis reflects thyroid hormone driven overactivity of the sodium potassium ATPase, amplified by the insulin surge after a carbohydrate load and by catecholamines, so small potassium doses restore power while non-selective beta blockade blocks the shift that caused it. Continuous cardiac and potassium monitoring is needed because the shifted potassium returns to the extracellular space as the episode terminates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange urgent nerve conduction studies before any replacement
options.rationale: Neurophysiology is used when an acute flaccid paralysis has no metabolic explanation, for example when Guillain Barre syndrome is suspected, and here a potassium of 2.1 mmol/L fully accounts for the weakness. Ascending paralysis with areflexia and albuminocytological dissociation would be the alternative picture, and delaying treatment to pursue it risks respiratory involvement and arrhythmia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is an uncommon but highly characteristic presentation of hyperthyroidism, disproportionately affecting young men of East and South East Asian descent, in whom thyrotoxicosis is otherwise more common in women. Attacks are precipitated by a high carbohydrate meal, strenuous exercise followed by rest, alcohol or stress, all of which drive potassium into cells through insulin and catecholamine stimulation of the sodium potassium ATPase that thyroid hormone has already upregulated. The weakness is proximal and symmetrical with preserved sensation and spares the respiratory and bulbar muscles in most cases, and it resolves within hours as potassium returns to the extracellular compartment. The essential management principle is that this is a redistribution rather than a depletion, so replacement is cautious and rebound hyperkalaemia is anticipated. Non-selective beta blockade with propranolol directly opposes the shift and is used both acutely and to prevent attacks until definitive treatment of the thyrotoxicosis takes effect.
key_points: Total body potassium is normal, so the deficit is redistribution rather than loss
Aggressive replacement causes rebound hyperkalaemia as the episode resolves
Propranolol blocks the catecholamine driven intracellular shift
Precipitants are carbohydrate loads, exercise followed by rest, alcohol and stress
Definitive treatment of the thyrotoxicosis prevents further attacks
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid function in every young adult presenting with hypokalaemic paralysis, because thyrotoxicosis may be biochemically obvious while clinically silent, with no goitre and no eye signs, and the attacks stop permanently once the patient is rendered euthyroid.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis

subtopic_detail: Young adult with hepatitis, new tremor and behavioural change with a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 24 year old man referred with 4 months of jaundice and abnormal liver tests. He drinks no alcohol, takes no supplements or herbal preparations, and has had no blood transfusions or tattoos.

His partner adds that for about 6 months his handwriting has become cramped and untidy, he has developed a tremor when holding a cup, and he has been uncharacteristically irritable and impulsive, losing a job he had held for 3 years.

data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen tip palpable, coarse postural and action tremor of both hands, mild dysarthria, no asterixis, no confusion
data_table.Investigations: ALT 180 units/L (less than 40), AST 210 units/L (less than 40), bilirubin 48 micromol/L (less than 20), alkaline phosphatase 42 units/L (30 to 110), INR 1.3, haemoglobin 104 g/L (130 to 180) with reticulocytosis, viral hepatitis serology negative, autoimmune and coeliac screens negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure ferritin and transferrin saturation with HFE genotyping
options.rationale: Hereditary haemochromatosis is a reasonable cause of unexplained liver disease, but it rarely produces clinical disease before the fourth decade, does not cause a movement disorder or personality change, and is associated with diabetes, arthropathy and skin pigmentation rather than haemolysis. It also would not explain the disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase. (Source: GESA: Abnormal liver function tests)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with gadolinium
options.rationale: Imaging will show basal ganglia changes if the diagnosis being considered is right, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to establish it and would not explain the liver disease. The diagnosis is made biochemically and confirmed at the slit lamp, with imaging used to characterise established neurological involvement. (Source: GESA: Abnormal liver function tests)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous liver biopsy as the initial investigation
options.rationale: Hepatic parenchymal copper quantification on biopsy is the confirmatory test when non-invasive results are equivocal, so biopsy has a role but not as the first step. Proceeding straight to a percutaneous procedure in a man with a prolonged INR adds bleeding risk before simple blood and bedside tests have been done. (Source: GESA: Abnormal liver function tests)

options.text: Measure alpha 1 antitrypsin level and phenotype the patient
options.rationale: Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency causes chronic liver disease in young adults and should be on the list, but it produces emphysema rather than a movement disorder and does not cause haemolytic anaemia. The neurological and psychiatric features are what make it a poor fit. (Source: GESA: Abnormal liver function tests)

options.text: Measure serum caeruloplasmin and arrange slit lamp examination
options.rationale: Liver disease with a movement disorder and personality change in a young adult, with haemolysis and an alkaline phosphatase that is low rather than raised despite cholestatic jaundice, is the recognised signature of hepatic copper overload. A low caeruloplasmin with Kayser Fleischer rings on slit lamp examination establishes the diagnosis in most patients, with 24 hour urinary copper added to complete the assessment. (Source: GESA: Abnormal liver function tests)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter causing copper accumulation in liver, brain, cornea and kidney, and it should be considered in any unexplained liver disease between about 5 and 40 years of age. Hepatic presentations range from asymptomatic transaminase elevation through chronic hepatitis to acute liver failure, while neurological presentations feature tremor, dysarthria, dystonia and parkinsonism, and psychiatric presentations feature personality change, impulsivity and mood disorder, often preceding the diagnosis by years. Two laboratory patterns are worth recognising: haemolytic anaemia from sudden copper release, and a paradoxically low alkaline phosphatase, since copper inhibits the enzyme, giving a low ratio of alkaline phosphatase to bilirubin that is particularly suggestive in fulminant presentations. Diagnosis combines low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and Kayser Fleischer rings, with liver biopsy copper quantification and genetic testing where results are equivocal. Treatment with chelation or zinc is lifelong and effective, and untreated disease is uniformly fatal, so first degree relatives must be screened.
key_points: Consider Wilson disease in unexplained liver disease between 5 and 40 years of age
Neurological and psychiatric features often precede recognition by years
A disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase with haemolysis is highly suggestive
Diagnosis combines low caeruloplasmin, raised urinary copper and Kayser Fleischer rings
All first degree relatives require screening because treatment prevents a fatal outcome
explanation.pearls: Kayser Fleischer rings are present in nearly all patients with neurological Wilson disease but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone, so their absence never excludes the diagnosis in a hepatic presentation.

subtopic_detail: Visible haematuria beginning within a day of a sore throat with normal complement levels
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 23 year old man whose urine turned the colour of cola yesterday. His sore throat began the day before that, and the urine change followed within 24 hours of the first symptom.

He had an identical episode a year ago during a chest infection, which cleared after three days and was not investigated. He has no flank pain, no dysuria, no fevers and no rash, has never smoked and takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema with no exudate, no peripheral oedema, no rash or purpura, no joint swelling, abdominal examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 3 plus and protein 1 plus, urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts, urine albumin creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol (less than 3.5), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60 to 110), C3 and C4 within normal limits, antistreptolysin O titre not raised, antinuclear antibody and ANCA negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to nephrology for consideration of a renal biopsy
options.rationale: Dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts localise the bleeding to the glomerulus, and the combination with significant proteinuria and hypertension in a young adult defines a nephritic presentation requiring histological diagnosis. Haematuria arising within a day or two of a mucosal infection, with normal complement, is the pattern of IgA nephropathy, and biopsy determines both the diagnosis and whether immunosuppression is warranted. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis
options.rationale: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows pharyngitis after a latent period of one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a raised antistreptolysin O titre, and both discriminators point the other way here. Antibiotics also do not alter the course of glomerulonephritis once it has developed. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Repeat the urine dipstick in three months and act on that
options.rationale: Observation is reasonable for isolated microscopic haematuria with normal blood pressure, normal renal function and no proteinuria. This man has an albumin creatinine ratio of 68 mg/mmol with hypertension and a second episode of visible haematuria, all of which mark a higher risk of progressive disease. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography urogram to find a bleeding source
options.rationale: Urological imaging investigates non-glomerular bleeding from stones, tumours or trauma, which produces isomorphic red cells without casts or significant proteinuria. Red cell casts effectively exclude a urological source and make irradiating a 23 year old unnecessary. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Refer for flexible cystoscopy to exclude a bladder lesion
options.rationale: Cystoscopy is indicated for visible haematuria in patients over 40, or younger patients with smoking or occupational risk factors, where urothelial malignancy is plausible. In a 23 year old non-smoker with glomerular red cells and proteinuria it investigates the wrong compartment entirely. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: The first decision in haematuria is whether the blood is glomerular or urological, and dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and significant albuminuria establish a glomerular source. Within glomerular disease, the temporal relationship to infection is the key discriminator: IgA nephropathy produces visible haematuria within one to two days of a mucosal infection, so it is described as synpharyngitic, while post-infectious glomerulonephritis follows a latent period of one to three weeks and consumes complement, giving a low C3. IgA nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, frequently presents in the second and third decades with recurrent visible haematuria, and carries a substantial lifetime risk of progression to kidney failure, which is why it is not a benign finding to observe. Adverse prognostic markers are proteinuria above 1 g per day, hypertension, reduced eGFR at presentation and specific histological features. Management centres on blood pressure control and maximal renin angiotensin system blockade, with SGLT2 inhibition and, for selected high risk patients, immunosuppression.
key_points: Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts identify a glomerular source
Haematuria within 1 to 2 days of infection suggests IgA nephropathy
A latent period of 1 to 3 weeks with low C3 suggests post-infectious glomerulonephritis
Proteinuria, hypertension and reduced eGFR mark higher risk of progression
Urological imaging and cystoscopy investigate the wrong compartment in glomerular bleeding
explanation.pearls: Quantify proteinuria in every patient with glomerular haematuria, because sustained proteinuria above 1 g per day is the single strongest modifiable predictor of progression in IgA nephropathy and is the threshold at which treatment intensifies.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent peptic ulceration with hypercalcaemia and amenorrhoea pointing to a familial endocrine syndrome
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with a fourth episode of epigastric pain and a duodenal ulcer found at gastroscopy. Helicobacter pylori was eradicated two years ago with confirmed clearance, and she takes a proton pump inhibitor daily and no anti-inflammatory medicines.

Separately she has not had a period for 2 years and reports occasional milky discharge from both breasts. Her father had kidney stones in his thirties and died at 54 from what the family were told was a tumour in his pancreas.

data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness, expressible bilateral milky nipple discharge, visual fields full to confrontation, no neck mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), parathyroid hormone 9.8 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), creatinine 76 micromol/L (45 to 90), prolactin 3960 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 1.7 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for parathyroidectomy and defer further investigation for now
options.rationale: Surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism will follow, but the operation differs when the disease is part of a familial syndrome, because all four glands are involved and a limited exploration leads to early recurrence. Deferring the syndromic assessment therefore risks the wrong operation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat Helicobacter pylori testing and re-treat if it is positive
options.rationale: Recurrent ulceration after documented eradication, in a patient taking no anti-inflammatory drugs, should prompt a search for acid hypersecretion rather than another eradication attempt. Proton pump inhibitor use also causes false negative urea breath and stool antigen testing. (Source: GESA: Peptic ulcer disease)

options.text: Refer for germline genetic testing and first degree family screening
options.rationale: Primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactin secreting pituitary tumour and recurrent duodenal ulceration from gastrin excess occurring together in a woman under 40, with a father who had stones and a pancreatic tumour, is a familial multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome until proven otherwise. Confirming the germline variant directs multigland parathyroid surgery, lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance, and predictive testing for relatives who are otherwise asymptomatic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence cabergoline and review the serum calcium in six months
options.rationale: Cabergoline is the correct treatment for a prolactinoma and will restore her periods, but treating one component in isolation leaves the hypercalcaemia untreated and the syndrome unrecognised. Six months is also too long to leave a corrected calcium of 2.82 mmol/L unreviewed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange gallium labelled somatostatin receptor imaging of the abdomen
options.rationale: Functional imaging localises neuroendocrine tumours and will be part of the assessment, but it is a localising study performed after biochemical confirmation of hormone excess, and fasting gastrin has not yet been measured. Imaging first can also be misleading, since small pancreatic lesions are common in this syndrome and not all are functional. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating variants in the MEN1 tumour suppressor gene, characterised by tumours of the parathyroid glands, the anterior pituitary and the pancreatic islets and duodenum. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the earliest and most common manifestation, affecting almost all patients by their fifties, and it is distinguished from sporadic disease by younger onset, multigland involvement and a family history. Gastrinoma causes recurrent, multiple or atypically sited peptic ulceration that persists despite eradication of Helicobacter pylori and standard acid suppression, and prolactinoma is the commonest pituitary lesion. The syndromic diagnosis changes management substantially: parathyroid surgery must address all four glands, lifelong surveillance for pancreatic and pituitary lesions is required, and predictive genetic testing allows presymptomatic relatives to enter surveillance. Hypercalcaemia also worsens gastrin secretion, so correcting the parathyroid disease often improves ulcer control.
key_points: Parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic or duodenal tumours define the syndrome
Hyperparathyroidism before 40 years, or with a family history, should prompt genetic assessment
Ulcers recurring after documented eradication without anti-inflammatory use suggest gastrin excess
Surgery must address all four parathyroid glands, unlike sporadic single adenoma disease
Germline testing enables predictive testing and surveillance for relatives
explanation.pearls: Measure fasting serum gastrin while the patient is off proton pump inhibitor therapy for at least a week where it is safe to do so, because acid suppression itself raises gastrin and is the commonest reason a gastrinoma result is uninterpretable.

sources.label: eviQ: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 genetic testing

subtopic_detail: Resuscitation strategy in septic shock complicated by severe fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 76 year old man brought in with rigors and confusion. He has severe aortic stenosis and is on the waiting list for transcatheter valve implantation, with a recent echocardiogram showing a valve area of 0.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 48 mmHg and preserved ejection fraction.

He has had 500 mL of compound sodium lactate and his first dose of intravenous antibiotics. Urine cultures have been sent and the source appears urinary. Your resident has drawn up a further 2 litres to complete a 30 mL per kilogram bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on 4 litres per minute, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds, jugular venous pressure 3 cm above the sternal angle, ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, bibasal crackles to the mid zones, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L from a baseline of 92 (60 to 110), haemoglobin 118 g/L (130 to 180), white cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
data_table.Bedside echocardiogram: Hyperdynamic hypertrophied left ventricle with a small end diastolic cavity, heavily calcified aortic valve, no regional wall motion abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his haemodynamic resuscitation?

options.text: Complete a 30 mL per kilogram crystalloid bolus over the next hour
options.rationale: The 30 mL per kilogram target is derived from populations without fixed outflow obstruction and is a starting point rather than an obligation. A hypertrophied ventricle with a small cavity has limited capacity to accept volume, and he already has crackles to the mid zones, so completing the bolus is likely to produce pulmonary oedema without increasing stroke volume across a fixed valve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give 250 mL boluses with reassessment and start early noradrenaline
options.rationale: With a fixed valve area the stroke volume cannot rise much whatever the filling, so perfusion depends on systemic vascular resistance and on the diastolic pressure that fills the hypertrophied myocardium, which makes an alpha agonist the physiologically correct support. Small aliquots with reassessment of the lactate, jugular venous pressure and lung fields preserve the narrow window between underfilling a stiff ventricle and flooding the lungs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start a dobutamine infusion to augment the cardiac output now
options.rationale: Inotropes are used in septic shock when there is myocardial depression with a low ejection fraction, and this ventricle is hyperdynamic with preserved function. Dobutamine also causes vasodilatation, which lowers the coronary perfusion pressure that a hypertrophied ventricle critically depends on. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give metoprolol 2.5 mg intravenously to slow the ventricular rate
options.rationale: Slowing the rate lengthens diastole and improves filling in severe aortic stenosis, which makes this superficially attractive, but his tachycardia is the compensatory response to sepsis and blunting it removes the only mechanism maintaining his cardiac output. Rate control belongs to a patient in atrial fibrillation who has lost atrial contraction, not to a septic patient in sinus rhythm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Restrict fluids entirely and start an intravenous frusemide infusion
options.rationale: Diuresis in a patient with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L and a rising creatinine worsens the underfilling of a stiff, non-compliant ventricle that depends on adequate preload to generate any stroke volume at all. The crackles reflect the limit of his tolerance to volume, not established fluid overload requiring removal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Severe aortic stenosis creates a fixed obstruction to left ventricular outflow, so stroke volume is largely determined by the valve area rather than by preload or contractility, and the compensating hypertrophied ventricle is stiff, small cavitied and dependent on adequate filling, sinus rhythm and a high diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion. Septic shock attacks every one of those dependencies at once, by vasodilating, by tachycardia shortening diastole, and by producing a state in which the usual answer is large volume resuscitation. The combination therefore sits in a narrow therapeutic window: too little volume underfills a non-compliant ventricle, while too much floods lungs that cannot be unloaded across a fixed valve. The resolution is to titrate small fluid aliquots against repeated clinical and echocardiographic reassessment and to restore perfusion pressure early with noradrenaline, whose alpha mediated vasoconstriction raises coronary perfusion without increasing the gradient. Source control and antibiotics remain the definitive treatment, and early intensive care involvement is warranted because these patients decompensate abruptly.
key_points: Stroke volume is fixed by the valve area, so perfusion depends on systemic vascular resistance
The 30 mL per kilogram target is a starting point, not an obligation in fixed obstruction
Noradrenaline raises coronary perfusion pressure without increasing the valve gradient
Compensatory tachycardia in sepsis should not be blunted with beta blockade
Small aliquots with repeated reassessment replace a single large bolus
explanation.pearls: Loss of sinus rhythm is catastrophic in severe aortic stenosis because atrial contraction contributes up to 40 per cent of filling in a hypertrophied ventricle, so new atrial fibrillation with haemodynamic compromise in this setting is an indication for prompt electrical cardioversion rather than rate control.
